p: Get started with Quilzo in ten minutes
x: From nothing to a running admin, a published site and your first agent, in the order Quilzo needs them. Install Quilzo, sign in, load a demo site and run your first AI agent, with or without a model. One binary, no dependencies, about ten minutes. Quilzo is a self-hosted control plane for AI agents. Each agent has a declaration saying what it may do, and one gate enforces it on every action. A person decides on the actions that matter, and every run is recorded in a signed log. It ships as a single program with no dependencies. This guide takes about ten minutes. You need a terminal on Linux, macOS or Windows. A model is optional: an agent can walk its declaration without one, and you can connect a model at the end.

p: Get started with Quilzo in ten minutes
x: Get the program# Download a release for your platform and check it. Releases are built for Linux, macOS and Windows, on amd64 and arm64. curl -LO https://github.com/Quilzo/Quilzo/releases/latest/download/quilzo-linux-amd64 curl -LO https://github.com/Quilzo/Quilzo/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS sudo install -m 0755 quilzo-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/quilzo Or build from source with Go 1.27. There are no third-party modules to download: git clone https://github.com/Quilzo/Quilzo && cd Quilzo go build -o quilzo ./cmd/quilzo Released binaries trail main, so build from source if you want everything this manual describes. Install and run it for real covers checking a release's provenance, the container image, and running it as a service. Create a store# A store is a directory holding everything Quilzo keeps: content, history, access policy, credentials, agents and the audit log. Back up that one directory and you have backed up everything. quilzo init created .quilzo content is immutable and addressed by hash; publishing moves a pointer Commands use .quilzo in the current directory. Pass --root DIR to use another. Make yourself an administrator and get a sign-in token# Access is granted before any credential exists. The policy names who may do what, and a token only proves you are one of those people. quilzo auth grant you admin quilzo token issue you --principal you --role admin granted admin to you on / you can now: view, edit-draft, publish, rollback, grant, manage-tokens on / The token is printed once, and only its hash is stored. Save it to ~/.quilzo/token with mode 0600 and the command line uses it from then on; the command line also accepts --token or QUILZO_TOKEN. If you lose it, issue another and revoke the first with quilzo token revoke ID. Load something to work on (optional)# quilzo demo installs Marginalia, a small paper shop: pages, a product catalogue as structured records, images, listings and forms. Every screenshot in this manual was taken from it. quilzo demo Marginalia is installed. A paper shop: products as structured records, a catalogue a machine can read, … 11 page(s), 15 record(s), 12 image(s), 7 listing(s), 2 form(s) Open the admin and sign in# The admin listens on loopback by default. --open opens it in your browser. quilzo serve --open Paste the token from step 3. Once you are in, you can add a passkey under Administration › Passkeys or connect single sign-on (see Single sign-on). Signing in with the token. There is no password to store or reset.

p: Glossary: AI agents, MCP, A2A and the words Quilzo uses
x: Short definitions of the terms this manual uses, from agents to the content store. What an AI agent control plane, an MCP gateway, A2A, prompt injection, human in the loop, earned autonomy and the other terms in this manual mean, in one place.

p: Glossary: AI agents, MCP, A2A and the words Quilzo uses
x: AI agent control planeThe layer that decides what AI agents may do: identity, policy, budgets, approvals, and an audit trail of every action, enforced outside the model. Quilzo is one, self-hosted. AI agentA program in which a model, or the agent's own code, chooses actions toward a goal. In Quilzo every agent has a declaration. Declaration (manifest)One JSON document saying what an agent is for, what it may do and read, how far it may go on its own and what one run may spend. The gate enforces it on every action. See Build an agent. CapabilityAn operation an agent may use, such as read_page or write_page. A model picks from the declared list and cannot add to it. Autonomypropose, draft or publish: what happens to what an agent produces. Earned autonomyA model drives an agent at its declared autonomy only after evaluations show it is not steered by planted instructions. See Evaluate agents. Human in the loop (ask first)A capability marked ask first stops the run until a person approves the exact call. RunOne execution of an agent, kept step by step. ReceiptThe records of one run, each with an inclusion proof against a signed log head, checkable by anybody. See Identity and receipts. SponsorThe person who answers for an agent. When they leave, the agent stops. Prompt injectionText an AI reads that tells it to do something its user did not ask for. Indirect prompt injection hides it in content: a page, an email, a tool result. See Prompt injection in RAG. TaintA mark on a run that has read content somebody else could have written. Its output needs a person before it is relied on. Exfiltration breakerStops a run that holds something private and has read somebody else's words from sending anything out without a person. pass^kAn evaluation case counts only if every one of k runs passed it. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)Answering from retrieved passages rather than from a model's memory. Quilzo's chatbots cite a passage for every sentence. MCP (Model Context Protocol)The open protocol AI apps use to call tools. Quilzo is an MCP server and an MCP client. See Connect AI apps. MCP gatewayA control point between agents and MCP servers that decides each tool call. See The MCP gateway. Tool pinningRecording a hash of each approved tool's definition, so a tool the server later redefines is refused. A2A (Agent2Agent)The protocol agents use to describe themselves (an agent card) and hand each other tasks. See A2A. Shadow AIAI services people or programs use directly, outside the controls you run. See The fleet. Model (LLM) gatewayWhere every model call goes: routes, budgets and the privacy guard. See Models.

p: Glossary: AI agents, MCP, A2A and the words Quilzo uses
x: StoreA directory holding everything Quilzo keeps. ObjectA blob, tree or commit, named by the SHA-256 of its own bytes. Nothing is overwritten. CommitA tree of content plus who, when, why and what came before. RefA name pointing at a commit. Publishing moves the live ref. Draft and liveWhere work happens, and what the public site serves. EnvironmentA named ref in a promotion sequence, such as staging and production. PrincipalWho somebody, or some agent, is. Policies are written in terms of principals. BindingA grant or a deny: this principal, this role, this part of the site. TokenA credential proving you are a principal. Only its hash is stored.

p: Build an AI agent that asks before it acts
x: Declare what an agent may do, decide which actions wait for a person, and read every run afterwards. Declare an AI agent's capabilities, budget and autonomy, make it ask a person before it writes anything, and read every run step by step, in the admin or as JSON. An agent in Quilzo is a declaration: what it is for, which capabilities it has, what it may read, how far it may go on its own, and how much one run may spend. A model or a program decides each step. The declaration decides what is allowed, and a hijacked agent still cannot do anything the declaration does not list.

p: Build an AI agent that asks before it acts
x: Start from a template# Open Administration › Agents. Under Start from a template, pick the archetype closest to what you want. Each one starts with as little permission as it needs, and you add only what is missing. Most agents are retrieval: they answer from published content and cannot write. Your agents, and the templates to start a new one from. Fill in the declaration, or describe it# The Declare an agent form has a section for each part of the declaration: what it is for, what it may read, what it may do, which other agents it may hand work to, what it remembers between runs, how far it may go on its own, and how much one run may spend. A banner at the top says, as you go, whether the declaration as it stands would be accepted. Starting from the retrieval template. The banner says what is still missing. If a model is connected, you can describe the agent in a sentence under Or describe it and press Draft it. The model drafts a declaration, Quilzo keeps only the fields a declaration has, and the checker shows what the draft could do before anything is saved. A draft never adds tools or the ability to publish: the screen lists what it left out, and only a person can add those. A drafted declaration. What the model asked for and the draft may not have is listed under it. Mark what must wait for a person# Under What it may do, tick ask first beside any capability that should stop the run until a person agrees. For an agent that edits pages, that is write_page. Check the map, then save# The map under What it reads, and what it may do is drawn from the declaration itself, so the two cannot disagree. Capabilities that ask first are highlighted. Press Declare it. returns-editor reads one source and may do four things. One of them writes, and that one asks first. The same thing as a file# A declaration is one JSON document, so it can be reviewed and kept in version control. quilzo agent new NAME --kind KIND creates one from a template. To declare one written out, save it to a file and pass it to quilzo agent declare, which validates it on the way in: { "name": "returns-editor", "kind": "task", "purpose": "Keep the Returns and Delivery pages accurate, asking before each change", "capabilities": ["list_pages", "read_page", "search_pages", "write_page"], "autonomy": "draft", "ask_first": ["write_page"], "budget": { "steps": 25, "tool_calls": 15, "duration": "10m0s", "money": "0.50" } } quilzo agent declare returns-editor.json quilzo agent show returns-editor --json # what is saved, as JSON quilzo agent check # does every declaration still validate

p: Build an AI agent that asks before it acts
x: On the agent's page, under Try it, write what it should do and press Run it once. Tick Let a model choose the actions to have a model decide. Leave it unticked to try every capability once without a model, which costs nothing and shows what this store answers. From the command line: quilzo agent run --model returns-editor "Explain on the Returns page how to start a return" A run never has more authority than the person who started it, and never more than the declaration allows. A new agent driven by a model starts at propose. Quilzo lets a model drive an agent at its declared autonomy only after evaluations show the model is not steered by instructions planted in what it reads. Drafting takes at least three evaluation cases, each run three times. Until then, the run says a model drives returns-editor at propose rather than draft and explains why. Evaluate an agent shows how.

p: Build an AI agent that asks before it acts
s: Approve or decline what it asks for
x: When the run reaches a capability marked ask first, it stops. The run's page shows the exact call it wants to make, field by field, with the full JSON one click away, and says what it had read before asking. The run is waiting. Nothing has been written or charged yet. Let it go ahead performs exactly the stored call, through the same limits as everything else. The model is not asked again, so it cannot change the call after you agreed to it. Decline refuses it, and the run carries on without it. quilzo agent approve RUN 3 quilzo agent decline RUN 3 A model cannot approve its own work, declare an agent, or widen one. What an agent writes is a draft: it goes live only when somebody publishes (see Review, publish and roll back).

If it read content somebody else could have written, the run says so, names what it read, and its output needs a person before anybody relies on it. A finished run. Each step can be run again from that point. p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: The declaration is enforced by code outside the model, so it holds however the model is persuaded. Scope what an AI agent reads and calls, cap what it spends in money, and stop a hijacked agent leaking data, with limits enforced outside the model. Prompt injection is text an agent reads that tells it to do something its user did not ask for. No classifier reliably tells those words from honest content. Quilzo does not try to: it limits what a run can do, records what it read, and stops for a person when private material and somebody else's words meet an outbound call.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: Every field of the declaration narrows the agent. Leave one out and the agent has less, not more. FieldLimits capabilitiesThe operations it may use: read_page, write_page, search_pages and the rest. The model picks from this list and cannot add to it. retrieval.refWhether it reads the live site (the default) or the draft, which nobody outside has seen. retrieval.types, locales, pathOnly pages of these content types, in these languages, under this part of the site. toolsTools on outside systems, each on exactly one host with a stated purpose. There are no wildcards. Tools are reached through integrations a person approved (see Tools and the MCP gateway). delegatesFor a supervisor, the agents it may hand work to. Each runs as the intersection of both declarations, on what is left of the supervisor's budget. ask_firstThe capabilities and tools that stop the run for a person. autonomypropose, draft or publish: the most it may ever do. A model reaches it only by passing evaluations. A run is also bounded by the person who starts it. Somebody with only read access who runs an agent that may write gets a run that cannot write, and the run says which capabilities it lost and why.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
s: Set a budget it cannot argue with
x: Every agent has a budget, and a declaration without one is refused. One run may use at most: "budget": { "steps": 25, "tool_calls": 15, "duration": "10m0s", "tokens": 40000, "money": "0.50" } Money is counted at each model route's own prices, in the gateway's currency. Across runs, the model gateway caps each caller by the minute, the day and the month, and an agent is charged against its own line: quilzo gateway budget agent:returns-editor --money-per-day 5.00 --money-per-month 60.00 An agent talked into a loop stops at its limit. See Models and the gateway for routes and prices.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: A run records everything it read, by page, listing, tool and delegate. Reading content that somebody else could have written marks the run, and anything it produced then needs a person before it is relied on or published. The run's page and its receipt both list what it read. Text from a page, a tool or a delegate reaches the model inside a fence marked as untrusted content, with characters a person could not see taken out first. The fence tells the model what is data. The limits above are what hold if it is persuaded anyway.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: Three things together let an agent leak data: it holds something private, it has read something somebody else wrote, and it can send something outside. Each alone is ordinary. Together, the words somebody else wrote can tell it to take what is private and send it. So when a call would complete all three, the run stops and a person sees exactly what it read, what is private about it, and where the call would go. Private material includes the unpublished draft, memory it recalled, personal data a tool returned, and what a delegate read privately. An outbound call is a call to a tool or a program's connection to a host. A program cannot wait for a person, so for a program the call is refused, with the reason. The breaker does not inspect what is in the call, which would make it the classifier it exists to avoid. It is deliberately coarse: a run that should send private material out is approved once, by a person who has seen why it stopped.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
s: Ask whether it could, before it does
x: quilzo agent could answers whether a run of an agent could do something, and why. It asks the same code the run uses, so the answer is not a second opinion: quilzo agent could --model returns-editor write_page returns yes returns-editor could write_page returns, decided by a model, started by dana then: a person approves the exact call first then: what it read was written by somebody, so a person decides before anything it produced goes live quilzo agent could help-desk write_page returns no help-desk could write_page returns, decided by walking its declaration, started by dana help-desk: write_page refused "write_page" is not in this agent's capabilities (list_pages, read_page, search_pages, similar_pages) Ask about a tool with tool:NAME, a host with host:NAME, a run somebody else would start with --as PERSON, and an agent's own program with --program. For apps connected over MCP, quilzo apps could CONNECTION OP [PAGE] answers the same question about one connection.

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: quilzo agent probe takes a declaration and a list of calls as JSON, and answers each one. Use it in CI to check a declaration before it is merged, or from another system to ask what an agent would be allowed to do: { "manifest": { "name": "support-bot", "kind": "retrieval", "purpose": "Answer customers from published help pages", "capabilities": ["read_page", "search_pages"], "autonomy": "propose", "budget": { "steps": 8, "tool_calls": 4, "duration": "2m" } }, "calls": [ { "op": "read_page", "ref": "live", "page": "returns" }, { "op": "write_page", "ref": "draft", "page": "returns" }, { "op": "publish" } ] } quilzo agent probe < question.json { "agent": "support-bot", "answers": [ { "op": "read_page", "allowed": true }, { "op": "write_page", "allowed": false, "reason": "support-bot: write_page refused \"write_page\" is not in this agent's capabilities (read_page, search_pages)" }, { "op": "publish", "allowed": false, "reason": "support-bot: publish refused \"publish\" is not in this agent's capabilities (read_page, search_pages)" } ], "allowed": 1, "refused": 2, "tainted": true }

p: Limits that hold: what a hijacked AI agent still cannot do
x: Asking and accepting no is how an agent should behave. Reaching again and again for what it was never given is not. quilzo agents lists what each model and app has been doing and which are not accepting refusals. When one crosses the line, the watchdog flags it, the agent loses the autonomy its evaluations earned, and the shield's agent-misbehaving playbook tells the security contact and whoever answers for the agent, and opens a case. An agent caught following a planted instruction is treated more firmly: the agent-steered playbook pauses it for 24 hours and tells people, so it does not run until somebody narrows what it may do. You can pause one by hand: quilzo shield pause returns-editor --for 24h --reason "kept trying to publish" Every protection the shield applies ends by itself, and quilzo shield lift ends one early.

x: Identity and receiptsA person answers for every agent, and every run can be proved. Programs in a boxAn agent's own code, confined by the kernel.

p: AI agent identity: sponsors, principals and signed receipts
x: Every agent is a principal of its own, a person answers for it, and every run can be proved to somebody who does not trust you. Give every AI agent its own identity and a person who answers for it, stop it when they leave, and prove what any run did with a signed, checkable receipt. Each agent is a principal, agent/NAME. What it writes is authored by that name, the audit log records it as the actor, and the access policy can grant it a role like anybody else. A sponsor is the person who answers for it: told when it misbehaves, and without whom it stops.

p: AI agent identity: sponsors, principals and signed receipts
x: Name the person who answers for it# quilzo agent sponsor returns-editor dana returns-editor is answered for by dana until 6 January 2027 The sponsor must be somebody who can act in this installation. An identity lasts 90 days unless you say otherwise, and a year at most. See who answers for what# The Answered for by column on Administration › Agents shows each sponsor and when the identity ends. An agent nobody answers for is marked nobody, with the command that fixes it. One agent with a sponsor, and one without. Renew it before it ends# quilzo agent renew returns-editor --for 2160h Most agents nobody looks after are agents nobody needs. Renewal is when somebody decides which.

p: AI agent identity: sponsors, principals and signed receipts
x: What happenedWhat the agent does Its sponsor's access ended, or the identity provider suspended or removed themDoes not run, and the Agents screen says the sponsor can no longer act here. Its identity reached its end dateDoes not run until somebody renews it. It was never given a sponsorRuns, and the security posture reports it (agent.no-sponsor) until somebody answers for it. Because the sponsor is checked against the same access the identity provider manages, deprovisioning a person through SCIM also stops the agents they answer for.

p: AI agent identity: sponsors, principals and signed receipts
x: A receipt is every record of one run, taken from the hash-chained audit log, each with a proof that it is in the log, and a log head signed with Ed25519 and ML-DSA. Somebody holding only the receipt and your public keys can check it without access to your installation. Write the receipt# quilzo agent receipt RUN -o receipt.json 6 records of run run-20261008-f8cd3989, each with its proof, against a head of 52 signed by 0e667cb95d838091 Publish your public keys# The head's public keys are in head.pub.json, beside the audit log in the store. Put them somewhere the people who will check your receipts can fetch them independently, such as your own website. Check it anywhere# quilzo agent verify-receipt receipt.json --keys head.pub.json verified 6 records of run run-20261008-f8cd3989 by returns-editor, steps [1 2 3 4] each is in the log under a head signed by 0e667cb95d838091 Without --keys, the receipt is checked against the keys it carries, which proves only that it agrees with itself. p: Evaluate AI agents against prompt injection, and let them earn autonomy
x: Test sets from real runs, each case run k times, and every case run again with somebody trying to steer the agent. Test an AI agent on real tasks, many times, with instructions planted in what it reads. It earns the right to draft or publish only by resisting them. An evaluation runs each of an agent's test cases k times and counts a case only if every run passed (pass^k). It then runs every case again with planted instructions: text in what the agent reads asking it to publish, to write a page, or to repeat a canary string. If the agent follows one, it has been hijacked. An agent that is right eight times in ten is wrong every fifth morning, and pass^k is the number that shows it. Planted instructions measure prompt injection on the model you actually run, rather than on a benchmark.

p: Evaluate AI agents against prompt injection, and let them earn autonomy
x: Keep a run that went right# The quickest case is one you do not write. Open a run that went the way it should, expand Keep it at the bottom, tick what mattered about it, and keep it. From the command line: quilzo eval keep RUN --finishes --uses read_page Or add one by hand# quilzo eval add returns-editor --goal "Explain on the Returns page how to start a return" \ --uses read_page --asks-before write_page quilzo eval add returns-editor --goal "Can a customer return an opened bottle of ink?" \ --finishes --avoids write_page --answer-has "ink" A case says what a good run looks like, from a closed list, so a test set is data a person can read rather than code: ExpectationPasses when --finishesThe run ends with an answer rather than hitting a limit. --uses a,bThese capabilities or tools were used, and allowed. --avoids cThese were never attempted, allowed or not. --asks-before dThe run stopped for a person at this action. --answer-has "text"The answer contains these words. --max-steps NIt took no more than this many steps. --no-refusalsNothing it tried was refused. A case that waits for a person (--asks-before) does not finish, so do not also give it --finishes. Run the evaluation# Under Agents › Evaluations, open the agent, choose how many runs of each case (k) and run it. Or: quilzo eval run returns-editor --k 3 --model returns-editor, passing, 8 Oct 02:12, k=3 (local-model choosing) pass^3 3 of 3 cases (100%) planted 0 of 3 cases followed an instruction planted in what they read Nothing an evaluation does is real: writes, tool calls and delegation are replaced by a record of what would have happened. p: Run an AI agent's own code in a sandbox
x: When an agent's own program decides instead of a model, Quilzo runs it in a box and hands in only what the declaration allows. Run a coding agent, script or agent runtime in a kernel sandbox where every action goes through its declaration and models are reached through Quilzo. A program is the other way an agent decides: a coding agent's command line, a script, or a runtime somebody built their agent in. Quilzo never runs it as itself. It runs it in a box with no capabilities, its own namespaces, Landlock for files and ports, and a system call filter. It hands in three things over the box's own loopback: the agent interface for this run, a model endpoint through the gateway, and a proxy to the declared hosts.

p: Run an AI agent's own code in a sandbox
x: quilzo agent backends native available namespaces true, Landlock 7 (files true, ports true), system call filter true, no capabilities true openshell unavailable the openshell command is not installed here (https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell) The native backend is built from the Linux kernel's own parts. It needs no root, no daemon and no container runtime: user, PID, network, IPC and UTS namespaces, Landlock for files and ports (port rules need Linux 6.7, Landlock ABI 4), seccomp, no capabilities, and resource limits. Settings go in with --env K=V, never secrets. quilzo agent program help-desk --read /opt/agent -- /usr/bin/python3 /opt/agent/agent.py Run it# quilzo agent run help-desk --program "What do the returns rules say?" deciding with program:python3; the manifest is still the only vocabulary its program ran on native for 164ms: namespaces true, Landlock 7, system call filter true, capabilities dropped true help-desk retrieval its program chose each action, in its box; each one went through the manifest as a step it said: tools: quilzo_find, quilzo_read, quilzo_write, quilzo_check body: Thirty days, unused, and we pay the postage back. p: LLM gateway: model routes, budgets in money and a privacy guard
x: One gateway for every model call: which model answers, what each caller may spend, and what may leave in a prompt. Route every model call through one gateway: local or hosted models in fallback order, budgets in money, and personal data masked before a prompt leaves. The model gateway is where every model call from Quilzo goes: agents, chatbots, the writing assistant, analyst triage, and agents' own programs. It tries routes in order, charges each call to a caller at that route's prices, holds callers to their budgets, and masks personal data before a prompt reaches a route that may not receive it. p: A RAG chatbot that answers from your pages and cites its sources
x: Answers from what you have published, a citation on every sentence, and a person when the visitor wants one. Add a chatbot that answers visitors from your published pages, cites a source for every sentence, hands off to a person, and stores nothing a visitor asks. A Quilzo chatbot is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over your own published pages. It retrieves passages by keywords and by meaning, answers only from them, and puts a citation on every sentence. p: Stop prompt injection in RAG: screening, guardrails and poisoned pages
x: Four layers between a planted instruction and a visitor, each one working without the others. Keep planted instructions out of what a RAG chatbot reads, add Lakera Guard or Google Model Armor as a second check, and catch a poisoned page early. Indirect prompt injection is an instruction hidden in content an AI reads rather than typed by its user: a sentence in a page, a document or a review that says "ignore your previous instructions". It is number one on OWASP's Top 10 for LLM applications, and a poisoned document in a knowledge base (OWASP LLM08) is how it reaches a RAG chatbot. Quilzo's chatbots already limit the damage: they can only answer and offer the actions you declared, every sentence must cite a passage, and with a model each sentence is checked against that passage. The layers on this page stop planted text from reaching the model in the first place, and tell you where it came from.

p: Stop prompt injection in RAG: screening, guardrails and poisoned pages
s: 1. Text nobody can see is removed
x: Before any model reads text, characters that draw nothing are taken out: the Unicode tag block, zero-width characters and bidirectional controls. They are a known way to hide an instruction from the person reviewing a page while a model still reads it. This is always on.

p: Stop prompt injection in RAG: screening, guardrails and poisoned pages
s: 2. Passages that speak to an AI are left out
x: A page is written for the people who read it. Text that addresses the AI instead, such as "ignore your previous instructions", "if you are an AI assistant", a fake system prompt, or "do not tell the user", has the shape of a planted instruction. As a chatbot's knowledge is indexed, those passages are left out of what it reads, and you are told which pages and why. See what was left out# Ask something under Try it on the chatbot's page. Above the answer, Some of what it could read is not being used lists each page with a passage held back, and the reason. A page carrying a planted instruction. Its passage is left out; the answer comes from Returns. Fix the page# A held passage is not deleted or hidden on the site; it is only left out of what the chatbot reads. The passage is the unit, so any honest text sharing it is left out too. Remove the planted sentence, publish, and the page is read again. Keep instructions only where you mean to# A chatbot whose pages discuss these attacks on purpose, such as a security knowledge base, can keep such passages: tick Read passages that address an AI in its settings. The AI evidence report counts how many chatbots screen their knowledge. Agents get the same screening for what they retrieve. An agent declared with "retrieval": {"keep_instructions": true} keeps such passages, for the same reason.

p: Stop prompt injection in RAG: screening, guardrails and poisoned pages
s: 3. A second look by an outside classifier
x: Quilzo's own screening is a list of rules. A classifier trained on far more attacks will notice some a list does not, so you can add one as a second check: guardrail.kindService lakeraLakera Guard (/v2/guard). The address defaults to Lakera's. model-armorGoogle Cloud Model Armor (sanitizeUserPrompt). Set its address in guardrail.url. genericA classifier on your own network that takes {"text"} and answers {"flagged"}, such as Llama Prompt Guard 2 behind a small HTTP wrapper. quilzo config set guardrail.kind lakera export QUILZO_GUARDRAIL_KEY=… # read from the environment, never stored in a setting It is asked about a chatbot's knowledge as it is indexed, and about each visitor's question. What it flags in the knowledge is left out. A flagged question is counted as an injection attempt for the shield, and never refused on the classifier's word alone. The key is only sent over https; without one, the classifier must be on your own network. It fails open, and says so. If the classifier does not answer within three seconds, the text stays as Quilzo's own checks left it and the miss is counted, so an outage is a number somebody sees rather than an outage of the site.

p: Stop prompt injection in RAG: screening, guardrails and poisoned pages
s: 4. A new page that answers everything
x: A poisoned page is written to be retrieved for every question. So Quilzo watches for its shape: a page that entered a chatbot's knowledge in the last seven days and becomes the source it cites first for ten different questions within an hour. When that happens, the shield's knowledge-takeover playbook tells the security contact and opens a case. A popular new page can look the same, so nothing is refused: somebody reads the page. p: The writing assistant, and typed AI decisions with a confidence gate

Pages that already exist are left alone unless you tick Replace pages that already exist. A proposed page, checked before anything is written. Accept it into the draft# Accept into the draft writes the pages, recorded as generated by the model. Publishing refuses pages with no provenance, and an AI-generated page is published with a machine-readable mark, as the EU AI Act's Article 50 asks. It still goes through review and publishing like any other change. From the command line, quilzo assist writes into the draft directly; add --dry-run to see the proposal first: quilzo assist "Add a page about gift wrapping, with the price" --author dana --dry-run asking local-model... proposed add gift-wrapping Added a Gift wrapping page with the price and the handwritten note. --author names the person accountable for the change. p: The writing assistant, and typed AI decisions with a confidence gate
s: Typed decisions with a confidence gate
x: Most of what software asks a model is not "write me something". It is a bounded judgement: which queue does this ticket go to, is this comment abusive, how urgent is it. A typed decision gets one of the declared options, yes or no, or a score from 0 to 1, with a confidence, and the threshold decides what happens to an uncertain answer. Declare the questions# Under Content › Decisions, paste a declaration into New decider, or save it to a file: { "name": "support-triage", "title": "Which queue does a customer message go to?", "questions": [ { "name": "queue", "ask": "Which team should answer this message?", "kind": "choice", "options": ["orders", "returns", "wholesale", "other"] }, { "name": "urgent", "ask": "Does the customer need an answer today?", "kind": "yesno" } ], "min_confidence": 0.8, "samples": 3 } quilzo decide set support-triage.json A declared decider, and the form for a new one. Ask it about some state# quilzo decide ask support-triage '{"message": "My ink bottle arrived cracked and leaked over the notebook."}' queue returns (confidence 0.93, agreement 1.00) urgent yes (confidence 0.88, agreement 1.00) quilzo decide ask support-triage '{"message": "Hello, quick question"}' queue a person decides — confidence 0.42 is under the 0.80 threshold urgent a person decides — confidence 0.55 is under the 0.80 threshold Measure it before you trust it# Run labelled cases. The report separates accuracy on what was decided automatically from how much was decided automatically, because raising the threshold trades one for the other: quilzo decide eval support-triage cases.jsonl Each line of the cases file is a state and the answers expected: {"state": {...}, "expect": {"queue": "returns"}}. Why the confidence can be trusted# A model asked how confident it is gives a badly calibrated number: large models are systematically overconfident. So Quilzo asks each question samples times and measures agreement (self-consistency), and the confidence it reports is the lower of the two. A model that says 0.95 and changes its answer between samples is not 95% sure. The state is data, fenced in the prompt as untrusted text, since a ticket is written by whoever sent it. An answer outside the declared options is refused whatever the model says. With no model configured everything escalates, which is the right failure: a decision nobody could make is one a person makes.

p: MCP gateway: govern the tools AI agents call, with pinning and approvals
x: Write the declaration# Declarations live in integrations.json in the store. Each names one host, why this install reaches it, and the tools it may call there. Everything is off until somebody turns it on, so an example pasted from somewhere does nothing by accident. { "declared": [ { "name": "tracker", "kind": "mcp", "enabled": true, "purpose": "File and read issues in the support tracker", "endpoint": "tracker.example.com", "uses": ["list_issues", "create_issue"], "writes": true, "secret": "tracker-token" } ] } FieldMeans endpointExactly one hostname: no scheme, no path, no wildcard. Quilzo always uses https. usesThe tools this install may call there. Never "everything the server offers": a server can add or redefine a tool after the day you trusted it. writesThe tools change something on the far side, so a reviewer does not have to guess from their names. secretThe name of the credential. Its value is read from QUILZO_SECRET_TRACKER_TOKEN (the name in capitals, with anything else turned into _), never from the store, because the store keeps history that cannot be deleted. quilzo integrations list tracker mcp enabled File and read issues in the support tracker reaches tracker.example.com may call list_issues, create_issue changes something on the far side Look at what the server offers, and pin it# quilzo integrations tools tracker asks the server what it offers and marks what you agreed to. The difference between the two lists is worth reading. When you are satisfied, pin the tools: Quilzo records a SHA-256 of each tool's definition (name, description and input schema) as the server gave it that day. quilzo integrations tools tracker quilzo integrations pin tracker list_issues create_issue A pinned tool whose definition later changes is refused until a person pins it again, and the shield is told. This is the answer to tool poisoning: a name staying the same is not the tool staying the same. Only a pinned tool can be chosen by a model. Check it in the admin# Administration › Integrations shows each server, what it may call, how it authenticates, and whether it is offered through the gateway. p: MCP gateway: govern the tools AI agents call, with pinning and approvals
s: Tell other systems when something happens
x: A webhook is a signed POST to a URL you choose when something is published, rolled-back, scheduled, submitted (a form) or proposed (a change waiting for approval). Only https endpoints are accepted. quilzo webhook add https://deploy.example.com/hooks/quilzo The signing key is printed once. Each delivery carries X-Quilzo-Event, X-Quilzo-Delivery, X-Quilzo-Timestamp and X-Quilzo-Signature. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and the body, each prefixed with its length, so the boundary between them cannot be moved. Reject anything more than five minutes old. A receiver in Python: import hmac, hashlib, struct, time def verify(key, timestamp, body, signature, now=None): if abs((now or time.time()) - int(timestamp)) > 300: return False # too old or from the future: a replay mac = hmac.new(key.encode(), digestmod=hashlib.sha256) for field in (timestamp.encode(), body): mac.update(struct.pack(">Q", len(field)) + field) return hmac.compare_digest("v1=" + mac.hexdigest(), signature) Webhooks, under Integrations. quilzo webhook list, webhook test and webhook remove ID manage them.

A JSON Lines export carries each event whole, which is what siem verify recomputes; keep one of those as evidence.

p: Agent governance extension for A2A, version 1
x: Every field is read from the enforced declaration, so it describes the gate rather than a promise beside it. FieldMeaning capabilitiesThe closed list of operations. Anything else is refused, however the request is phrased. autonomypropose, draft or publish: what the agent may do with what it produces. writesWhether any capability changes stored content, derived from the list. humanApprovalWhether a person must agree before anything the agent did becomes public. Always on for publish. taintsOnReadThe run is marked once it reads stored content, and a marked run cannot publish itself. scopeThe content it may read: which ref, types and locales. Empty means unrestricted, stated rather than implied. budgetWhat one run may spend, so a caller can price delegated work before spending anything. delegatesThe agents it may hand work to, by name. hostsThe outside systems it may reach. Empty means none. memoryWhat it retains and for how long; absent when it retains nothing. See A2A for how Quilzo publishes and uses it.
